issues.legal_issue: The interim head of a Part B State could exercise the State Legislature’s constitutional powers where that head was the authority functioning as the State’s legislature immediately before the Constitution commenced.
material_facts: Before the Constitution commenced, the governing covenant vested the United State’s legislative authority in its Rajpramukh, who could promulgate measures having the force of law.
No State Legislative Assembly had been constituted and summoned when the challenged land-reform law was enacted.
The covenant separately assigned the Rajpramukh an executive power to resume jagirs, and the challengers argued that this restricted his legislative power.
issues.conclusion: The Rajpramukh was competent to enact the law under Article 385. In the covenant, “Ordinance” meant a law, and the executive power concerning resumption did not restrict the separate legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: Article 385 empowered the body or authority functioning immediately before the Constitution as the legislature of the corresponding State to exercise the constitutional powers of the State Legislature until the new legislature was constituted. Articles X(3), VII(3) and XIX of the Covenant of the United State of Rajasthan had to be read in context: Article X(3) vested legislative authority in the Rajpramukh, “Ordinance” meant a law having the force of an Act, and Article VII(3) concerned executive resumption powers rather than restricting legislative authority. Article 385 did not require that the prior legislative authority have possessed unlimited powers.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: A person challenged the validity of a law enacted by a State authority.
predicates.interim_state_legislature_not_constitute: The State’s legislature under the Constitution had not yet been constituted and summoned when the law was enacted.
predicates.prior_legislative_authority_vested_in_he: The governing arrangement in force before the Constitution commenced vested the State’s legislative authority in its head.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a State law enacted before the new State legislature is constituted, and the prior governing arrangement vested legislative authority in the State’s head, the head had interim legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A bill drafted by ministers could satisfy the interim constitutional requirement that the Rajpramukh prepare it when he adopted it as his own by endorsing his approval.
material_facts: The Bill was initially drafted in the Ministerial Department and approved by the Council of Ministers.
The Rajpramukh signed an endorsement of approval on the Bill and separately reserved it for the President’s consideration.
A revised Bill was prepared after the President withheld assent to an earlier version; the Rajpramukh approved and reserved the revised Bill, to which the President assented.
issues.conclusion: The Rajpramukh was not required to draft the Bill personally. His signed endorsement of approval established its adoption, so the requirement of Article 212-A(2) was met; the procedural objections also failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 212-A(2) required the Rajpramukh to prepare the Bill, but did not require him personally to draft it. He could adopt a ministerially drafted Bill, provided he decided its essential policy questions. In context, his signed endorsement of approval signified adoption; further inquiry into whether his state of mind was legislative or executive was inadmissible. The Court also held that the President’s earlier order withheld assent and that the later submission was a fresh Bill.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_interim_bill: A person challenged a law on the ground that the required interim procedure for preparing a bill had not been followed.
predicates.bill_initially_drafted_by_ministers: Ministers or their department drafted the bill before it was placed before the State’s head.
predicates.head_signed_approval_and_reserved_bill: The State’s head signed an endorsement approving the bill and reserved it for the required further consideration.

issues.definition: When a bill drafted by ministers is challenged for failure to satisfy the interim preparation procedure, the State head’s signed approval and reservation of it means the preparation requirement was satisfied.

issues.legal_issue: A law taking jagir interests under the State’s sovereign power, rather than enforcing rights under the original grants, is in substance a law of acquisition even if it describes the taking as resumption.
material_facts: The law authorized the State to take jagir lands notwithstanding existing jagir law and extinguished the holders’ rights, title and interests in them.
The taking was not based on breach of grant conditions or another ground for resumption under the applicable grant or general law.
The law provided for compensation and transferred the interests to the Government.
issues.conclusion: In pith and substance, the law provided for acquisition and fell within the State legislative power over acquisition in Entry 36 of List II, notwithstanding its use of the term “resumption.”
issues.legal_principle: The distinction between resumption and acquisition turns on the source and nature of the taking: resumption ordinarily rests on pre-existing rights under a grant, while acquisition involves taking through sovereign eminent domain. The pith and substance of the legislation, not its label, controls. The compensation scheme supported the conclusion that the taking was acquisition. Although the law also related to land and land tenures under Entry 18 of List II, the specific acquisition entry, Entry 36 of List II, applied.

predicates.state_legislative_competence_challenged: A person challenged whether the State had legislative authority over the subject of a law.
predicates.state_takes_property_under_sovereign_pow: The law transfers or extinguishes private interests through the State’s sovereign power rather than through a private-law transaction.
predicates.taking_is_not_enforcement_of_grant_right: The State does not rely on breach of the grant or another pre-existing legal right to take the property.

issues.definition: When legislative competence is challenged and a State takes property through sovereign power rather than enforcing rights under a grant, the law is treated as acquisition within State legislative power.

issues.legal_issue: For constitutional protection of land-reform laws, “jagir” includes grants conferring land-revenue rights on persons who are not tillers of the soil, including maintenance grants.
material_facts: The tenure term had come to be used both popularly and in legislative practice for grants conferring rights in respect of land revenue, not only for its original military-service grants.
The challenged law sought to abolish intermediaries and establish a direct relationship between the State and the tillers of the soil.
Some grants were made for maintenance to people who did not cultivate the land.
issues.conclusion: “Jagir” in Article 31-A had the wider, contemporary meaning and covered grants under which holders had rights in respect of revenue but were not tillers of the soil, including maintenance grants.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A was intended to protect legislation abolishing intermediaries and establishing a direct relationship between the State and cultivators. The word “jagir” was to be read according to its popular and legislative usage at the time, rather than confined to its historical military-service meaning. A grant of revenue rights to a non-cultivator could therefore be a jagir for Article 31-A.

predicates.constitutional_land_reform_protection_at: A party disputed whether a land-reform law fell within constitutional protection for laws concerning land tenures or grants.
predicates.tenure_confers_land_revenue_rights: The tenure gives its holder rights in respect of land revenue.
predicates.holder_is_not_a_tiller: The holder does not cultivate the land as a tiller.

issues.definition: When constitutional protection for a land-reform law is disputed, a revenue-rights tenure held by a non-tiller counts as a jagir for that protection.

issues.legal_issue: Tenures originating in conquest or other arrangements could qualify as jagirs or similar grants when later sovereign recognition or legislation gave them the character of grants.
material_facts: The holders of one tenure had acquired lands by conquest, but continued in possession after acknowledging the later ruler’s sovereignty and paying an annual sum; the State and its laws subsequently recognized the holders as jagirdars.
Holders of another tenure continued in possession after a later ruler established sovereignty, subject to military service and quit rent.

A land-revenue enactment declared State ownership and deemed proprietary interests, including the relevant tenure, to be held as grants; another enactment defined holders’ revenue rights as rights granted by the ruler.
Other holders had entered possession as lessees or grantees and were later recognized as permanent holders or subordinate chiefs.
issues.conclusion: The relevant Bhomichara and Bhumia holdings were protected as jagirs or similar grants, and the Shekhawati and subeguzar holdings were grants within Article 31-A. A grant need not be express, and a legislative grant can qualify as well as a grant made by a sovereign.
issues.legal_principle: A jagir must originate in a grant, but the grant may be implied from the sovereign’s recognition of continued possession after establishing sovereignty. A person who acknowledges the new sovereign is a subject, not a partly sovereign intermediary. Legislation may alter or define proprietary interests and may create a legislative grant; for Article 31-A, it makes no difference whether the grant derives from sovereign prerogative or legislation. The Court relied on Vajesinghji Joravar Singji v. Secretary of State and Secretary of State v. Sardar Rustam Khan on the effect of acquisition of sovereignty, and on the relevant Marwar and Mewar land-revenue enactments and legislative practice.

predicates.constitutional_land_reform_protection_at: A party disputed whether a land-reform law fell within constitutional protection for laws concerning land tenures or grants.
predicates.continued_possession_recognized_by_sover: A later sovereign or a law recognized the holder’s continued possession or defined the holder’s land rights.
predicates.tenure_characterized_as_a_grant: The relevant history or law treated the holder’s interest as arising from an express, implied or legislative grant.

issues.definition: When a land-reform protection dispute concerns continued possession recognized by a sovereign or law and characterized as a grant, the tenure is a jagir or similar grant for that protection.

issues.legal_issue: A later enactment by the same sovereign authority could displace an earlier constitutional instrument to the extent the two were inconsistent.
material_facts: An earlier instrument made by the ruler provided protections concerning property and equality.
A later land-law enactment by that same ruler declared State ownership of land and defined the rights of holders of specified tenures.
The later enactment was inconsistent with the earlier instrument to the extent relevant to the challenged land rights.
issues.conclusion: The later enactment repealed or modified the earlier instrument to the extent of inconsistency, and the challenge based on the earlier instrument failed.
issues.legal_principle: Where the same authority enacted both instruments, its later enactment could repeal or modify the earlier one insofar as they were inconsistent. The Court applied that principle to the earlier Mewar constitutional provisions and the later Mewar Government Kanoon Mal Act.

predicates.challenge_relies_on_earlier_instrument: A party relies on an earlier constitutional or legal instrument to challenge a later enactment.
predicates.same_authority_enacted_later_inconsisten: The authority that made the earlier instrument later enacted a law inconsistent with it.

issues.definition: When a challenge relies on an earlier instrument and the same authority later enacted an inconsistent law, the later law displaces the earlier instrument to the extent of the inconsistency.

issues.legal_issue: A land-reform law protected by Article 31-A could not be invalidated on grounds concerning compensation, public purpose or equality, and the challenged law in any event did not fail on those grounds.
material_facts: The law acquired jagir interests and provided compensation based principally on income, with additional rehabilitation grants and other benefits.
The holders argued that compensation was inadequate, that there was no public purpose, and that the law discriminated by permitting resumption on different dates.
The law made all jagirs liable to resumption, conferred no discretionary power to exempt selected jagirs, and allowed different classes to be resumed on different dates for practical reasons.
issues.conclusion: The compensation, public-purpose and equality objections were barred by Article 31-A. The compensation provisions were not shown to be illusory or a device to take property without payment; the law served a public purpose, and the uniform liability of jagirs to resumption did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A barred challenges to a protected acquisition law based on Part III, including Article 31(2) and Article 14. A protected law could still be attacked as a fraud on the Constitution if its true intention were to take property without payment and its compensation provisions were merely illusory. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh, Visveshwar Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjea, Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Biswambhar Singh v. State of Orissa. It held that the law served a public purpose and that different resumption dates for practical and administrative reasons were not discriminatory.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_acq: A person challenges a law that acquires property on grounds concerning compensation, public purpose or equality.
predicates.land_reform_law_is_protected: The acquisition law concerns land tenures or grants within the relevant constitutional protection for land reform.
predicates.compensation_provisions_are_not_illusory: The law provides compensation or other meaningful benefits and the evidence does not show that these are merely a device to take property without payment.

issues.definition: When a protected land-reform acquisition law is challenged and its compensation provisions are not illusory, objections concerning compensation, public purpose and equality do not invalidate it.

issues.legal_issue: A permanent lease that is neither a jagir nor an enumerated similar tenure cannot be resumed under a statute limited to those tenures.
material_facts: The disputed estate had been granted on a permanent lease, with the holders enjoying its income while paying a fixed annual amount.
The grant was not made for services and did not assign a right to collect land revenue.
The annual assessment was not nominal, and the evidence did not establish the features of the specified permanent quit-rent tenure.
The statute’s definition covered jagirs and listed tenures, but did not cover this kind of permanent lease.
issues.conclusion: The estate was a permanent lease rather than a jagir or the specified permanent quit-rent tenure. The resumption notification concerning it was outside the statute and unauthorized; the same conclusion applied to interests derived by sub-grant from that estate.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory definition and enumerated tenures govern the reach of the resumption law; a general land-reform purpose cannot expand the expressed definition. The Court distinguished an istimrari tenure, whose essential features included a nominal and permanent quit rent, from a permanent izara lease. The sub-grantees’ rights followed the status of the original lease.

predicates.challenge_to_resumption_notification: A holder challenges a notification purporting to resume the holder’s land under a resumption law.
predicates.tenure_is_permanent_lease: The holder’s interest derives from a permanent lease rather than a grant of land-revenue rights or services.
predicates.tenure_is_not_enumerated_or_qualifying_g: The tenure does not fall within the law’s listed categories or otherwise qualify as a jagir or similar grant.

issues.definition: When a resumption notification is challenged and the tenure is a permanent lease outside the law’s covered categories, the notification is unauthorized.

issues.legal_issue: Property established to be dedicated to religious worship or service falls within the statute’s express exemption from resumption.
material_facts: The holder of a small grant alleged that its income was dedicated to the worship of religious deities and that the holder used it for religious services.
The State did not deny that allegation, and the Court found the dedication established.
issues.conclusion: The property was exempt from resumption under the statute, and the notification concerning it was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: The resumption chapter expressly excluded jagirs whose income was used for maintaining a place of religious worship or performing a religious service. The Court applied that statutory exemption after finding the dedication established.

predicates.challenge_to_resumption_notification: A holder challenges a notification purporting to resume the holder’s land under a resumption law.
predicates.property_income_dedicated_to_religious_w: The property’s income is dedicated to maintaining a place of religious worship or performing a religious service.

issues.definition: When a resumption notification is challenged and the property’s income is dedicated to religious worship or service, the property is exempt from resumption.
